w: Henry VIII raised this artillery fort in 1540 to guard the Fal estuary against French and Spanish fleets. Its keep answered Civil War cannon fire a century later - Royalists held out until a long 1646 siege broke them. Reinforced against Napoleon, rearmed twice more against the Luftwaffe, it stood down only in 1956.
s: Tudor fort that outlasted Napoleon and the Luftwaffe
_facts: Built by Henry VIII 1540-42 as part of the King's Device programme
Defended the Carrick Roads/River Fal
Held by Royalists in the Civil War, taken after a long 1646 siege
Modernised in the 1730s and 1790s against French invasion fears
Rearmed in WWI and WWII, saw action against the Luftwaffe
Decommissioned in 1956

w: Built in 1750 as a coaching inn to change horses on the long haul across Bodmin Moor, it moonlighted - so the legend goes - as a warehouse for a smuggling ring. Daphne du Maurier borrowed its name and story for her 1936 novel, filmed by Hitchcock in 1939, though the inn itself never let the cameras in.
s: The smugglers' inn that inspired du Maurier's novel
_facts: Built 1750 as a coaching inn, staging post for changing horses
Historical association with smuggling on Bodmin Moor
Setting for Daphne du Maurier's 1936 novel Jamaica Inn
Adapted into Hitchcock's 1939 film, though the inn itself was not used as a filming location
Referenced in a 2005 Tori Amos song written driving the Cornish cliffs

w: Raised as an earthwork castle soon after 1068 and rebuilt in stone as seat of the earldom of Cornwall, it spent its final centuries as a prison - inmates nicknamed it Castle Terrible for the brutal conditions. The last prisoners left for Bodmin Gaol in 1842; the ruins became a park.
s: The Norman castle that ended its days as Castle Terrible
_facts: Established by Brian of Brittany after 1068 as an earthwork and timber castle
Administrative centre of the earldom of Cornwall, rebuilt in stone in the 12th century
Became a gaol and site of executions, nicknamed Castle Terrible
Captured by rebels in the 1549 Prayer Book Rebellion
Closed as county gaol by 1842 and landscaped into a park

w: Sir Richard Edgecumbe fought for Henry Tudor at Bosworth Field and came home with money and a manor to show for it - Cotehele is the granite and slate house he built from 1485, barely changed in five centuries since. The National Trust keeps its Tudor rooms much as time left them, above the tidal Tamar.
s: A Tudor manor built on Bosworth Field winnings
_facts: Medieval house with Tudor additions in the parish of Calstock
Built by the Edgecumbe family from 1485 after the original manor house was demolished
Sir Richard Edgecumbe fought for Henry Tudor at the Battle of Bosworth
Little changed over five centuries; now owned by the National Trust
Granite and slate manor on the banks of the River Tamar

w: Local legend has Joseph of Arimathea landing here with the young Christ - some scholars go further, arguing this speck a mile off Looe is Ictis, the tin-trading island the ancient Greeks wrote of. Now a wildlife reserve, it's reachable only by licensed boat, its waters a marine conservation area since 1995.
s: The island legend says Joseph of Arimathea once landed on
_facts: Also known as St George's Island, a mile off Looe
Legend that Joseph of Arimathea landed here with the Christ Child
Some scholars propose it as Ictis, a pre-Roman tin-trade centre
Owned and managed by the Cornwall Wildlife Trust as a nature reserve
Part of the Whitsand and Looe Bay Marine Conservation Area, established 1995

w: Cecil Williamson's collection of folk magic, ceremonial regalia and Wiccan relics was run out of Windsor and Bourton-on-the-Water by outraged locals before settling in Boscastle in 1960. His resident witch, Gerald Gardner, split off to run a rival museum - this one has since grown into the largest of its kind anywhere.
s: The world's largest collection of witchcraft artefacts
_facts: Founded by folk magician Cecil Williamson in 1951, originally on the Isle of Man
Gerald Gardner was resident witch before the pair fell out and he bought that museum
Williamson's rival museum faced opposition at Windsor and Bourton-on-the-Water
Settled permanently in Boscastle in 1960
Sold to Graham King in 1996; described as the largest such collection in the world

w: A 1620s manor above the River Fowey, rebuilt almost wholesale after an 1881 fire tore through it - only the parish church in its grounds kept its older bones. That church, dedicated to St Hydroc, still rings a bell cast around 1599, alongside eight Victorian companions in its battlemented tower.
s: A grand manor rebuilt from the ashes of an 1881 fire
_facts: Country house and 890-acre estate above the River Fowey
Dates from the 1620s; interiors mostly rebuilt after an 1881 fire
National Trust since 1953, Grade I listed
Parish church of St Hydroc stands in the grounds, parts dating to the late 15th century
Church has nine bells; the ninth dates to around 1599

w: A granite tor crowning Bodmin Moor, ringed by a Neolithic enclosure and studded with Bronze Age hut circles - people gathered on this outcrop for thousands of years before a war memorial joined the summit. A logan stone still rocks somewhere in its jumble of granite, for anyone patient enough to find it.
s: A moorland tor ringed by Bronze Age hut circles
_facts: Tor on Bodmin Moor with a Neolithic tor enclosure
Site of numerous Bronze Age hut circles
Summit holds a logan stone and a war memorial

w: A Cold War hunter-killer submarine, in Royal Navy service from 1971, now sits open as a museum ship at the Devonport Naval Heritage Centre. Step inside a boat built to shadow Soviet submarines through the North Atlantic - plans are underway to grow the site into a full Cold War centre around her hull.
s: Climb aboard a retired Cold War hunter-killer sub
_facts: Churchill-class nuclear fleet submarine in Royal Navy service from 1971
Decommissioned and now a museum ship at the Devonport Naval Heritage Centre
2021 plans to build a Cold War Centre around the vessel, backed by the National Museum of the Royal Navy

w: Rows of vast dish antennas turned skyward on Goonhilly Downs made this the largest satellite earth station on the planet at its peak, beaming transatlantic calls and television down from orbit. BT still holds the site on a 999-year lease, its dishes now landmarks on a peninsula built for fishing boats.
s: A field of giant satellite dishes on the Lizard
_facts: Large radiocommunication site on Goonhilly Downs, Lizard peninsula
Once the largest satellite earth station in the world, with 30+ antennas
Owned by Goonhilly Earth Station Ltd under a 999-year lease from BT Group
Also links into undersea cable lines

w: Robert, Count of Mortain, raised this motte-and-bailey fort on the bones of an older Roman post soon after 1066, giving the Normans a watch over the Lynher River within a generation of the Conquest. Its 12th-century keep still stands sentinel above the water, a quieter cousin to the more famous Restormel Castle.
s: A Norman motte-and-bailey built over a Roman fort
_facts: Motte-and-bailey castle built probably by Robert, Count of Mortain, soon after the Norman Conquest
Built on the ruins of an earlier Roman fort
12th-century keep, similar in style to Restormel Castle
Caput of the feudal barony of Trematon, overlooks the Lynher River

w: Silvery-grey Pentewan stone and warm brick colonnades make this early 18th-century house one of Cornwall's quieter National Trust showpieces, its lawns running down toward the River Lynher. Grade I listed and little altered, it draws none of the crowds that swarm its grander cousins further east.
s: A Georgian country house of Pentewan stone and brick
_facts: Early 18th-century property in the care of the National Trust
Located between Torpoint and the village of Antony
Grade I listed; faced in silvery-grey Pentewan stone with colonnaded brick wings
Overlooks the River Lynher

w: Standing at the southernmost tip of mainland Britain, this lighthouse has long been the first welcome home for ships working up the Channel - on a clear night its beam has been logged from 100 miles out. Lizard Point itself is one of Cornwall's great set-pieces, cliffs dropping into some fierce tidal water.
_facts: Lighthouse at Lizard Point guiding vessels through the English Channel
Long served as a welcoming beacon for ships returning to England
On a clear night the light has reportedly been seen from 100 miles away

w: Henry VIII's engineers built this clover-leaf fort in 1540 to work with Pendennis across the water, each covering the other's blind spots along the Fal estuary. Royalist to the end of the Civil War, it surrendered only in 1646, then kept modernising against Napoleon and France again, guns falling silent after 1905.
s: Henry VIII's clover-leaf fort guarding the Fal
_facts: Artillery fort built by Henry VIII 1540-42, clover-leaf design with three bastions
Partnered with Pendennis Castle to defend the Carrick Roads/River Fal
Held by Royalists in the Civil War, surrendered in 1646
Redeveloped in the 1850s against fears of France, guns retired after 1905

w: A 26-acre sub-tropical ravine garden tumbling to the Helford River, planted with palms and giant gunnera that feel plucked from somewhere far warmer than Cornwall. Its neighbour Glendurgan shares the same sheltered valley and the same trick of climate - both exploit a fold in the land that keeps the frost away.
s: A sub-tropical ravine garden above the Helford River
_facts: 26-acre sub-tropical garden near Glendurgan Garden, above the Helford River
Part of the parish of Mawnan
